clue.text: After suspension, wonder about marks received by drunken fighter

indicators.note: the rest of the clue comes after the word for suspension, so it follows on

parts.note: a ban is a suspension, as from playing

indicators.note: something received by another is taken inside it, so the drunken word holds the rest

parts.note: tight is slang for drunk

indicators.note: about means around, so the wonder word goes round the marks

parts.note: awe is wonder
M is short for marks, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A boxer, back from a ban, is amazed at the bruises a drunken opponent left on him.
explanation.walkthrough: AWE goes 'about' M to make AMWE, and that is 'received by' TIGHT: T-AMWE-IGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: A bantamweight is a boxer in a light weight class, so a kind of fighter.

clue.text: Look angry as major port sends nothing out east

indicators.note: the port sends a letter away, the first half of a removal signal
with sends, out says the nothing letter is put out of the port's name

parts.note: Bristol is a major port in south-west England
O looks like zero, nothing
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Someone bristles because a big port has dispatched nothing to the east.
explanation.walkthrough: BRISTOL is a big port city in south-west England; 'sends nothing out' drops its O, leaving BRISTL, and E is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To bristle is to show anger or irritation, as hackles rise on an animal.

clue.text: New and splendid singlet, very green

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, written AI in crosswords
a vest is a singlet, a British sleeveless undershirt

explanation.surface: A shop describes a smart new singlet in a very bright green.
explanation.walkthrough: A1, 'first-rate', is taken as the letters AI. A vest in British English is an undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Green means inexperienced or gullible, and the most gullible person is the naivest.

clue.text: Creature's limb faulty — fuss about it

parts.note: an arm is a limb

indicators.note: the fuss word goes about, around, the faulty word that 'it' points back to

parts.note: ado is fuss
ill can mean bad or faulty, as in ill-made

explanation.surface: An animal has a damaged leg, and there is a lot of fuss about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' points back to 'faulty', which is the part ADO goes 'about'.
explanation.definitionFit: An armadillo is an armoured burrowing mammal of the Americas, so a creature.

clue.text: Squeeze right through part of plane

indicators.note: the right letter runs through, inside, the plane part

parts.note: a wing is part of an aeroplane

explanation.surface: Someone squeezes themselves right through a gap in an aircraft's structure.
explanation.definitionFit: To wring something is to twist and squeeze it, as with wet washing.

clue.text: He'll offer cover version finally, one much more likely to go out

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word version

parts.note: surer means more certain, more likely

explanation.surface: A singer's cover version, at the end, is the one most likely to be dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover version' reads as one phrase but splits: 'cover' ends the definition. The charade runs I, N, SURER, so 'one' comes before the N in the answer; 'to go out' rounds off the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurer is a company that provides cover against loss in return for premiums.

clue.text: One breaks the law putting cowl on chimney

indicators.note: in a down clue the cowl word sits on top of the chimney word

parts.note: a cowl is a hood
lum is a Scottish and northern English word for chimney

explanation.surface: Someone is breaking the rules by fitting a cowl to a chimney.
explanation.walkthrough: A cowl is also a cap fitted to a chimney, which makes the surface plausible. LUM is the Scots word for chimney.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoodlum is a gangster or thug, someone who habitually breaks the law.

clue.text: Drink after drink shatters her good faith

indicators.note: to shatter something is to break it into pieces, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Drinking one glass after another destroys a woman's trust.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is wittier than it looks: the drink taken after a night's drinking.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for a morning drink taken to ease a hangover from the previous night's drinking.

clue.text: Article I am repeating about singular religious belief

parts.note: an is the indefinite article

indicators.note: the repeated pair goes about, around, the singular letter
the contracted form of I am appears twice in a row

parts.note: I am contracts to I'm, letters IM
S is the grammar abbreviation for singular

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson: an article, a repeated 'I am' and the singular, then a religious creed.
explanation.walkthrough: IM repeated is IMIM; S goes inside the second pair: IMI-S-M.
explanation.definitionFit: Animism is the belief that spirits live in natural objects, a religious belief.

clue.text: Dressed to show the knees, almost — I omit the details

indicators.note: almost means the phrase stops one letter short of its end

parts.note: someone wearing shorts shows the knees, so is in shorts

explanation.surface: Someone describing an outfit cuts the story short: the knees were on show.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used to sum up briefly, skipping the details, as in 'to cut a long story short'.

clue.text: Nerd shows wizard how to do it

parts.note: with 'how to do it' this means teaches, trains
Harry Potter is the boy wizard of the children's books

explanation.surface: A geek demonstrates to a magician how a trick is done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows ... how to do it' together means TRAINS, with 'wizard' between them as the one being taught.
explanation.definitionFit: A trainspotter is a hobbyist who logs locomotive numbers, a byword in Britain for an obsessive nerd.

clue.text: One much improved in rubber is to have another walk-over

definitions.meaning: a worn tyre given a new rubber tread is remade and improved
to walk over again, to tread a second time

explanation.surface: A rubber player who has got much better is due another easy win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rubber' looks like a series of games, and 'walk-over' like an easy victory; both are literal here.
explanation.definitionFit: A remoulded tyre is so named, and the verb form means to tread the same ground once more.

clue.text: Travel by water with a brutal man

parts.note: to go is to travel
a rill is a small stream of water

explanation.surface: Someone goes by boat with a thug for company.
explanation.definitionFit: Gorilla is slang for a big, violent thug, by comparison with the great ape.

clue.text: Bases host large ships

indicators.note: to host is to have inside, so the bases word holds the large letter

parts.note: feet are the bases things stand on
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Naval bases are home to big vessels.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleet is a body of ships under one command.

clue.text: Guild member's organ on which many play

parts.note: the liver is an organ of the body

indicators.note: playing with the word many shuffles its letters

explanation.surface: A guild member owns a church organ that lots of people play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' wants to be a church instrument; it is the body organ. The livery companies are the old trade guilds of the City of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A liveryman is a full member of a City of London livery company, the historic trade guilds.

clue.text: Reveal Ben may come to like Bede

indicators.note: the letters may come to form something else once rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone named Ben may turn out like the Anglo-Saxon monk Bede.
explanation.definitionFit: Bede, the eighth-century English monk and historian, is known by the title the Venerable Bede.

clue.text: Passes — are they at one's side?

definitions.meaning: passes on to the next generation, bequeaths
with arms relaxed, the hands hang down at your sides

explanation.surface: A question about where someone's passes or cards are kept.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb form 'hands down' means passes on; the second reading pictures hands literally lowered.
explanation.definitionFit: To hand down is to pass on to a successor, and lowered hands rest at one's side.

clue.text: By touring college, finds a sort of family

indicators.note: the by word tours round, encircling the college letters

parts.note: by means near, as in 'stand by me'
UCL is University College London

explanation.surface: Near a college, someone discovers a particular kind of family.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuclear family is the core unit of parents and children.

clue.text: Corps eating each starter for breakfast with seconds; there's no meat course

indicators.note: the corps letters take in, eat, the following letters

parts.note: the SAS is the Special Air Service, a British army corps

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Soldiers eat breakfast and want seconds, though no meat course is served.
explanation.walkthrough: SAS 'eating' EA and B gives S-EAB-AS, then S for seconds.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish of this fish makes a fish course, so a course with no meat in it.

clue.text: A month in which we do cleaning

indicators.note: the month abbreviation is the one in which the we letters sit

parts.note: Sep is short for September

explanation.surface: There is a month set aside for spring-cleaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To sweep a floor with a broom is to do cleaning.

clue.text: No end of fuss, in the main, creating poetic structure

indicators.note: the shortened fuss word goes in the main

parts.note: the main is an old term for the open sea

indicators.note: the fuss word loses its final letter

parts.note: a stink is a fuss, as in 'kick up a stink'

explanation.surface: Endless commotion at sea produces a poem with a set form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No end of fuss' looks like 'lots of fuss'; it means STINK without its K.
explanation.definitionFit: A sestina is a poem of six six-line stanzas with repeating end-words, a fixed poetic form.

clue.text: Stare hard at what's in orbit

definitions.meaning: to look hard and closely at someone
the orbit is the eye socket of the skull

explanation.surface: A puzzle about staring at a satellite in orbit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orbit' wants to be space; it is the eye socket.
explanation.definitionFit: To eyeball someone is to stare at them, and the globe of the eye sits in the socket called the orbit.

clue.text: Artist offers tea: drop round

indicators.note: the drop word goes round the tea word

parts.note: to dump is to drop
cha is slang for tea

explanation.surface: A painter offers tea and invites someone to drop round.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel Duchamp was the French artist known for his readymades such as Fountain.

clue.text: Philosopher's books mount up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, books of the Bible
an alp is a mountain

explanation.surface: A philosopher's pile of books grows taller.
explanation.definitionFit: Plato was the ancient Greek philosopher, pupil of Socrates.

clue.text: Particular relaxation inhibits muscle

indicators.note: to inhibit is to hold in, so the relaxation word holds the muscle

parts.note: rest is relaxation
a pec is a chest muscle

explanation.surface: A specific kind of relaxation stops a muscle working.
explanation.definitionFit: A respect is a particular aspect or detail, as in 'in every respect'.

clue.text: Wander round about north area in island

indicators.note: the wander word goes round the next letters

parts.note: to gad about is to wander
re means about, concerning
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A wanderer roams around the northern part of an island.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenada is a Caribbean island nation in the Windward Islands.

clue.text: Armed force's equipment in terrible shape at the end

indicators.note: the equipment word sits in the terrible word

parts.note: bad means terrible
a rig is a set of equipment

indicators.note: only the end letter of shape is used

explanation.surface: An army's kit is in dreadful condition.
explanation.definitionFit: A brigade is a military unit of several battalions, an armed force.

clue.text: World's neatly parcelled out —— this divides the country

indicators.note: the letters are divided up and dealt out again in a new order

explanation.surface: The world is neatly divided up, and here is the thing that splits the land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'country' means countryside, not a nation. Walls of stones without mortar divide fields in rural Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Walls built of stones without mortar mark field boundaries across the British countryside.
